chapter: Heroes, rivals and the drummers' craft
title: Never studying drums: flash chimes, tympani and Freddy Albright
summary: Crawford says his chimes and tympani were for show, he learned to read through nerve, and he studied late with Freddy Albright.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Yeah, but I've had a tympani also, but I never had no education on it. I didn't study no drums until I was with a Broadway musical, from Freddy Albright. He was a good teacher, good stick man. He was older than I, and every time he -- well, he was chosen to be the drummer, and -- with one of the symphonic leaders --
-- Toscanini, somebody like that. He was that technical. And I used to study from him when I finally started to studying. He was highly recommended by other percussionists, people like that.
Well, now, since you didn't -- would you have these -- all of this equipment that you hadn't studied how to play it, would -- did you -- you played it, though?
Well, they were up there for a flash. I really didn't know how to play them, but I knew how to hit a chime note and a tympani note or something like that, which
Lunsford's band was no symphony band, wanted to be a swing band. And so I knew, if they wrote the part, I'd play it.
Now, you -- you were reading music then at that time when you were with Lunsford's band?
Had you learned how to read music in high school?
No. Every little bit of help I got was just through my nerve. That's all.

Technique on drum, I didn't have no technique, but I played. My job to me was to lift that band, just lift it right off the floor and push it. That was what all I -- all I knew. Would you care for something to eat?
